glossary.def: NASA's workmanship standard for cables, harnesses and wiring; lacing is §9.2

glossary.quote: 9.2 Lacing for Trunk, Branches, and Breakouts. 9.2.1 When engineering documents specify the use and type of lacing, the following requirements shall apply.

glossary.def: The first stitch: a spot tie with a running end

glossary.def: A clove hitch followed by a square knot

glossary.def: Two crossed turns round the bundle
glossary.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
glossary.quote: a clove hitch followed by a square knot as shown in Figure 9-2

glossary.def: Ties the clove hitch's two ends off
glossary.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
glossary.quote: a clove hitch followed by a square knot

glossary.def: The long end that laces on

glossary.def: One tape along the bundle in running lockstitches
glossary.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring

chapters.title: Why lace, and the starting stitch

lines.caption: Lace the cables to the hose
lines.spoken: Loose cables on a LowRider flap, snag and chafe, and can yank a plug mid-cut.

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: "Harness designs and routing shall provide support and protection to harnesses and cables so that they are protected from abrasion, cold flow, cut through, vibration, chafing, flexing, and sharp edges."

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: "Provision shall be made for stress relief in wires entering connectors from harnesses"

lines.uncited: "flap" and "snag" are the tutorial's own (the picture shows the loose cables swaying); "yank a plug" is the tutorial's reading of NASA §7.2.28's stress relief at connectors; which cables ride with the core is shown, not said (d19: the problem in one line, the reveal sooner)

lines.spoken: The fix? Cable lacing: the method NASA specifies for its mission hardware.

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: "This standard applies to production and processing of mission hardware"

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: "Continuous lacing shall be achieved using running lockstitches as shown in Figure 9-5."

sources.title: Wikipedia, Cable lacing
sources.says: "Cable lacing is a method for tying wiring harnesses and cable looms, traditionally used in telecommunication, naval, and aerospace applications."

sources.title: Wikipedia, Cable lacing
sources.says: "Some organizations have in-house standards to which cable lacing must conform, for example NASA specifies its cable lacing techniques in chapter 9 of NASA-STD-8739.4."

lines.spoken: Tight, tidy, tough: one tape, no sharp zip-tie tails, and one cut stitch won't unravel the rest.

sources.title: NAVSHIPS 900171, Electronic Installation Practices Manual, Chapter 9 Cabling, Section 7 Lacing and Binding
sources.says: "the \"over and under\" form is necessary to prevent unraveling of entire cable lacing, in the event one or more stitches are cut"

lines.uncited: "tight, tidy, tough" and "no sharp zip-tie tails" are the tutorial's own

lines.caption: Start by the last zip tie
lines.spoken: Following NASA's lacing standard, start beside the core's last zip tie with a spot tie round all three.

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: "Harnesses laced with single tape shall initially be tied with a starting stitch." "Single-tape starting stitches shall be the same as a spot tie with a running end or as shown in Figure 9-1 View A."

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: "Spot ties shall consist of a clove hitch followed by a square knot as shown in Figure 9-2 or other non-slip knots."

sources.title: Wikipedia, Cable lacing
sources.says: "Some organizations have in-house standards to which cable lacing must conform, for example NASA specifies its cable lacing techniques in chapter 9 of NASA-STD-8739.4."

lines.caption: Clove hitch: two crossed turns
lines.spoken: Two turns, the second crossing over the first, ends tucked under the cross: a clove hitch grips without slipping.

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: "Spot ties shall consist of a clove hitch followed by a square knot as shown in Figure 9-2 or other non-slip knots."

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.where: Fig. 9-2 View A (read from the figure)
sources.says: "CLOVE HITCH": two crossed turns round the bundle

lines.uncited: "Grips without slipping" is the tutorial's wording; NASA §9.2.5 only calls the spot tie's knots non-slip ("or other non-slip knots").

lines.caption: Right over left, left over right
lines.spoken: Secure it with a square knot: right over left, then left over right, pull snug, and trim the short end.

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: "Spot ties shall consist of a clove hitch followed by a square knot as shown in Figure 9-2 or other non-slip knots."

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: "CLOVE HITCH AND SQUARE KNOT"

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: "Lacing tie-ends shall be trimmed."

sources.title: WireCare, Tying a marline hitch with lacing tape
sources.says: "Snug the knot tight and trim the short end to about 1/8" or so."

lines.uncited: "Right over left, then left over right" is the common way to tie a square knot; no surveyed source spells it out.

lines.caption: Wrap once, loosely
lines.spoken: Each lockstitch begins with one loose turn of tape round the hose and both cables.

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: "Continuous lacing shall be achieved using running lockstitches as shown in Figure 9-5."

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: each running lockstitch is one turn round the bundle

lines.caption: Over, then under the turn
lines.spoken: Bring the end back over its standing part, then under the turn; one cut stitch won't unravel the rest.

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.where: Fig. 9-5; Fig. 9-3's running lockstitch (read from the figure)
sources.says: the end crosses over the standing part, then under the turn's start

sources.title: US Navy rate-training manual 14160 (title not checked), marline hitch
sources.says: "Just remember that the end of the line goes over the standing part and under the round turn so that it binds itself."

sources.title: NAVSHIPS 900171, Electronic Installation Practices Manual, Chapter 9 Cabling, Section 7 Lacing and Binding
sources.says: "the manner in which the lock stitch is made may vary, but the "over and under" form is necessary to prevent unraveling of entire cable lacing, in the event one or more stitches are cut"

sources.title: Wikipedia, Cable lacing
sources.where: Cable lacing, continuous lacing (cites Bureau of Naval Weapons 1962, pp. 7-9 to 7-14, not read)
sources.says: "A series of half-hitches, while visually similar, is not recommended for this application."

lines.caption: Pull it tight
lines.spoken: Pull the end along the hose; the loop closes down and grips the bundle.

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: "Continuous lacing shall be achieved using running lockstitches as shown in Figure 9-5."

sources.title: NAVSHIPS 900171, Electronic Installation Practices Manual, Chapter 9 Cabling, Section 7 Lacing and Binding
sources.says: "The stitch used in keeping the conductors together under pressure is the lock stitch."

lines.caption: Lockstitch every 68 mm (2.7")
lines.spoken: Repeat along the hose: one lockstitch every 68 millimetres, each pulled snug before the next.

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: "Continuous lacing shall be achieved using running lockstitches as shown in Figure 9-5."

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: "Lacing stitches and spot ties shall be placed as detailed in Table 9-1."

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: harness larger than 25.4 mm (1.00 in): maximum distance between harness ties 76.2 mm (3.00 in)

lines.caption: Round the U-turn and back
lines.spoken: Keep the same spacing round the U-turn and back along the lower run, the tape flat on top.

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: "Lacing stitches and spot ties shall be placed as detailed in Table 9-1."

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: harness larger than 25.4 mm (1.00 in): maximum distance between harness ties 76.2 mm (3.00 in)

sources.title: WireCare, Tying a marline hitch with lacing tape
sources.says: "Keeping the lacing tape as flat and free of twists as possible"

lines.caption: Never over 76 mm (3") apart
lines.spoken: Never leave more than 76 millimetres between stitches, or the cables sag away from the hose.

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: harness larger than 25.4 mm (1.00 in): maximum distance between harness ties 76.2 mm (3.00 in)

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: "Lacing stitches and spot ties shall be placed as detailed in Table 9-1."

lines.uncited: "Or the cables sag away from the hose" is the tutorial's reason; NASA states the spacing with no reason.

lines.caption: Last lockstitch at the breakout
lines.spoken: Just before the sleeve leaves the hose, the breakout, tie one last lockstitch.

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: "The separation of a conductor or group of conductors from the main body of wires in a harness."

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: "Lacing shall be terminated at every major breakout or branch" (25 to 30 percent or more of the wire volume); "Closing and starting stitches at branches and breakouts shall be next to the breakout."

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: "Lockstitching shall terminate with a closing stitch before each large breakout or branch of the harness."

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: the closing stitch: "LOCKSTITCH PLUS TWO HALF HITCHES"

lines.caption: Two half hitches lock the end
lines.spoken: Then two half hitches round the tape behind it lock the end, so the lacing can't work loose.

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: "Single or double lacing tape shall be terminated with a closing stitch as shown in Figure 9-3."

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: the closing stitch: "LOCKSTITCH PLUS TWO HALF HITCHES"

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: the two half hitches are tied round the tape's own standing part between the running lockstitch and the last lockstitch

lines.uncited: "So the lacing can't work loose" is the tutorial's reason; NASA gives the closing stitch's form (Fig. 9-3), not its purpose.

lines.caption: Pull snug, trim the end
lines.spoken: Pull them snug and trim the single tie-off end short.

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: "Lacing tie-ends shall be trimmed."

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: one tape throughout; its one free end is labelled "TIE-OFF END"

sources.title: NASA-STD-8739.4A, Workmanship Standard for Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring
sources.says: acceptance: "Lacing terminated with a closing stitch and ends trimmed."

chapters.title: The laced bundle, and a tip

lines.caption: One bundle, moving together
lines.spoken: Now watch the core travel: the hose, cord and sleeve flex together, held by every stitch along the run.

sources.title: NAVSHIPS 900171, Electronic Installation Practices Manual, Chapter 9 Cabling, Section 7 Lacing and Binding
sources.says: "When the conductors are properly laced, they support each other and make a single, neat cable."

lines.uncited: "Held by every stitch" describes the picture; no source states it.

lines.spoken: One last tip: lace with the hose already in its working bend, and keep the tape flat, never twisted.

sources.title: NAVSHIPS 900171, Electronic Installation Practices Manual, Chapter 9 Cabling, Section 7 Lacing and Binding
sources.says: "When bends occur in cable runs, always make the bend before lacing, to keep the bend in place (Figure 9-65)."
